source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.1 (PDF 73, printed 70). The GCD steps and the Halting Problem proof sketch are general computer-science knowledge, flagged for review. MCQ 3 and long question 2 are answered.

items: Solvable: an algorithm can solve it in a finite amount of time, with clear inputs and outputs and a step-by-step procedure. Example: the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers by the Euclidean algorithm.

Unsolvable: no algorithm can solve it in all cases. Example: the Halting Problem, deciding whether a given program will eventually halt or run forever; Alan Turing proved no general algorithm can solve it for all program-input pairs.

blocks.text: The Euclidean algorithm replaces the pair (a, b) by (b, remainder of a / b) until the remainder is 0: GCD(48, 18): 48 = 2 x 18 + 12, 18 = 1 x 12 + 6, 12 = 2 x 6 + 0, so the GCD is 6. Before tackling a complex problem, first check that it is solvable; this saves time and resources (Tip).

blocks.prompt: Which is true for unsolvable problems (MCQ 3)?
blocks.explanation: (b) they cannot be solved by any algorithm.

blocks.prompt: Explain why the Halting Problem is unsolvable and its implications (long question 2).
blocks.explanation: Suppose a program H could always decide whether any program halts on any input. Build a program D that asks H about D itself and then does the opposite: if H says D halts, D loops forever; if H says D loops, D halts. Either answer from H is wrong, so H cannot exist (Turing's argument by contradiction). Implications: no tool can check every program for infinite loops, some questions about programs can never be answered automatically, and computers have fundamental limits.

items: Solvable: an algorithm finishes in finite time (GCD of 48 and 18 is 6).
Unsolvable: no algorithm works for all inputs (Halting Problem, Turing).
